state.misconception_label: Struggles to visualise nets of 3D shapes

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This is the net of a... ![A circle touching a sector](). I got Triangle because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were trying to wrap a present in wrapping paper. Would the way you fold and cut the paper give you the shape of the box or object you're wrapping?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get what you mean about the wrapping paper, but I'm still confused. So, if I cut and fold it a certain way, it should look like the shape of the box? But how does that relate to the net I saw? I thought it was just a triangle because of the way it looked.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were trying to fold origami to make a box. Would the way you fold and crease the paper create the shape of the box you're trying to make? Even though the net may look like a triangle, think about how folding and unfolding it could create a 3D shape.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get that the net is like a flat version of the shape, but I still don’t see how it can make a box if it looks like a triangle. So, if I folded it differently, would it still be a triangle, or would it change into something else? How do I know what the net should look like for different shapes?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses generic analogies (wrapping paper, origami) that don't address the specific net shown (circle touching sector, which forms a cone), and the student becomes more confused, ending with more questions than they started with.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (wrapping presents, folding origami) to help the student understand the abstract concept of geometric nets, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
